title: Research
text:
This paper studies how the construction of the historical information set affects measured exchange-rate predictability. I distinguish information available at the forecast origin from information assigned to the same economic reference period but observed only later.
Using a pseudo-real-time panel of 14 USD exchange rates, I compare traditional macroeconomic fundamentals with market-based predictors under alternative information-alignment rules. The results show that alignment effects are small for traditional macroeconomic specifications but substantially larger in specifications containing S&P 500 information.
The paper interprets this contrast as a measurement issue: forecast performance depends not only on which variables enter a model, but also on which realization of those variables the historical forecaster was actually allowed to observe.
Keywords: Exchange rates, forecasting, information sets, real-time data, machine learning

title: Research
text:
Dissertation

When Long-Run Evidence Fails: Adjudication, Failure Modes, and Detectability
This chapter examines whether exchange rates exhibit stable long-run relationships with macroeconomic fundamentals once integration properties, structural breaks, deterministic specifications, and model admissibility are treated as part of the empirical evidence.
Across 14 USD exchange rates, no currency obtains primary support for a common four-variable long-run specification. The absence of support arises through several distinct empirical channels, including direct lack of cointegration evidence, integration ambiguity, deterministic-specification sensitivity, and dynamic misspecification.
The chapter also studies whether slow economic adjustment may make economically meaningful relationships difficult to detect in finite samples.



Unit of Analysis and Pooled Identification
This chapter asks whether pooling information across currencies can recover structural or predictive content that is difficult to identify in individual exchange-rate models.
The analysis changes the unit of estimation while holding the underlying data construction fixed, providing a bridge between the long-run and forecasting evidence in the preceding chapters.
Work in progress.

title: Projects
section: Independent Validation of a GARCH Volatility Model
text:
Independent Validation of a GARCH Volatility Model
Focus: Market Risk · Model Validation · VaR Backtesting
Independent validation of a GARCH(1,1) volatility model using S&P 500 and EUR/USD daily returns.
Key components:

Conceptual soundness and parameter diagnostics
Independent re-implementation of the GARCH likelihood
Benchmarking against EWMA, Student-t GARCH, GJR-GARCH, EGARCH, and Historical Simulation
95% and 99% one-day VaR backtesting
Kupiec and Christoffersen coverage tests
Basel traffic-light analysis
Parameter stability and stress-period analysis
Optional Black-Scholes pricing extension to study volatility-model risk transmission

Skills: Python, time-series econometrics, VaR, Expected Shortfall, model benchmarking, implementation verification, sensitivity analysis
Status: In development

title: Projects
text:
Point-in-Time Financial Data Governance Pipeline
Focus: Data Risk · Backtesting Infrastructure · AWS
A point-in-time financial data pipeline designed to prevent look-ahead bias and reconstruct the information actually available at each historical forecast origin.
Key components:

FRED / ALFRED real-time vintage data
PostgreSQL point-in-time database
Release-date-aware joins
Publication-lag and revision analysis
Automated schema, integrity, coverage, and outlier checks
Comparison of final-vintage versus historically available data
AWS deployment using S3, RDS PostgreSQL, Lambda, EventBridge, and CloudWatch
Least-privilege IAM and reproducible data lineage

Skills: SQL, PostgreSQL, AWS, data engineering, data governance, look-ahead controls, model-input validation
Status: In development

text:
Independent Validation of a Retrieval-Augmented LLM System
Focus: AI Model Validation · RAG · Model Governance
A validation framework for a retrieval-augmented generation system built on public regulatory and model-risk documents.
Key components:

Manually verified evaluation set with in-scope, out-of-scope, and adversarial questions
Retrieval evaluation using Recall@k and MRR
Generation evaluation using faithfulness, citation accuracy, answer relevance, and hallucination rates
Prompt-sensitivity and non-determinism testing
Chunk-size and context-ordering sensitivity
Failure taxonomy separating retrieval, generation, and corpus failures
Self-hosted RAG system compared with a managed vendor implementation
Model Card, Validation Report, and Monitoring Plan

Skills: LLM evaluation, RAG, AI model risk, Python, AWS Bedrock, S3 Vectors, model governance

title: About
text:
I am a Ph.D. candidate in Economics at the CUNY Graduate Center, with a background in financial engineering and international economics.
My research focuses on exchange rates, macro-financial forecasting, time-series econometrics, and machine learning. Across my dissertation work, I study how empirical conclusions about exchange-rate predictability depend on long-run identification, information timing, and the unit of analysis.
Alongside my academic research, I am developing applied projects in model validation, data governance, quantitative risk, and AI model risk.
